# Chapter 5 · Concatenation: the operand gets escaped, both ways > **Enters as:** `Markup('
')`, with `'

& '` waiting on the right of a `+` The page is finished. What follows in the scenario is a smaller, blunter exercise: building a footer by gluing three pieces together with `+`. It matters out of proportion to its size, because in real application code this is the shape most mixing takes — a safe fragment, a plain string, another safe fragment — and it happens without anyone thinking about escaping at all. First the literal `'
'` goes through the constructor the story met in chapter 1: `Markup.__new__` with `encoding=None`, which checks for `__html__` (a plain `str` has none), skips the decoding branch, and hands the text straight to `str.__new__` ([`__init__.py#L122-L131`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L122-L131)). No escaping. The developer wrote those angle brackets and means them; the trace returns `Markup('
')`. Python then evaluates the two `+` operators left to right, so this `Markup` is the left operand of the first one. ## The right operand is escaped, not trusted `Markup.__add__` is four lines ([`__init__.py#L136-L140`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L136-L140)). It first asks whether the operand is something that can become markup at all: `isinstance(value, str) or hasattr(value, "__html__")`. The payload `'

& '` is a `str`, so the guard passes. Had it been, say, an `int`, `__add__` would return `NotImplemented` and Python — finding no `int.__radd__` that accepts a `Markup` — would raise `TypeError`. That is deliberate: a `Markup` will not silently stringify arbitrary objects into your document. The operand is then passed through `self.escape(value)`, the classmethod from the last chapter ([`__init__.py#L230-L240`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L230-L240)), which calls the module-level `escape`. This time the fast path applies — `type(s) is str` is exactly true ([`__init__.py#L39-L40`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L39-L40)) — so `_escape_inner` runs over the characters and the trace shows the constructor receiving `'</p> & <script>oops</script>'`. Look at what happened to the bare ampersand in the middle. In the pure-Python implementation, `&` is replaced *first*, before the four replacements that themselves introduce `&` ([`_native.py#L1-L8`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/_native.py#L1-L8)). Reverse that order and the `&` of every freshly-written `<` would be escaped again into `<`; the whole string would come out double-escaped. The ordering is the entire correctness of that function, and the C version encodes the same thing differently, by writing each replacement directly to an output buffer in one pass ([`_speedups.c#L18-L72`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/_speedups.c#L18-L72)). With the operand now inert, `__add__` calls `super().__add__(...)` — ordinary string concatenation — and wraps the joined text in `self.__class__`, not in a hard-coded `Markup` ([`__init__.py#L138`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L138)). The trace records the constructor call with `'
</p> & <script>oops</script>'` and returns it as a `Markup`. The footer's own tag survived; the payload's did not. ## Safe plus safe is not escaped twice The second `+` has `Markup('
')` on the right — built, like the first literal, by a plain constructor call at trace line 74. It goes through exactly the same door: the guard passes (a `Markup` is a `str`), and `Markup.escape` is called on it. Inside, the familiar round trip: `type(s) is str` is false for the subclass, the `__html__` branch is taken, `Markup.__html__` returns `self` ([`__init__.py#L133-L134`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L133-L134)), the constructor calls `__html__` once more on the way in, and `'
'` emerges with its tag intact. Concatenating safe to safe costs an allocation and changes nothing. That idempotence is what lets application code use `+` freely without tracking which side has already been escaped. The final constructor call yields `Markup('
</p> & <script>oops</script>
')`, and `print(repr(...))` runs it through `Markup.__repr__`, which prefixes the class name so the value reads as markup rather than as a string in the output ([`__init__.py#L167-L168`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L167-L168)). One road not taken here: had the plain string been on the *left* — `"

& …" + Markup("
")` — Python would still reach MarkupSafe, because for a subclass operand it tries the reflected method first, and `Markup.__radd__` escapes the left operand before adding ([`__init__.py#L142-L146`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L142-L146)). Direction does not matter; the test for it is one line long ([`tests/test_markupsafe.py#L13-L16`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/tests/test_markupsafe.py#L13-L16)). > **For the owner:** The `str` API on `Markup` is not uniformly escaping, and the split is worth knowing before you sign off. Methods that *insert* text escape their argument: `join` escapes every element ([`__init__.py#L170-L171`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L170-L171)), `replace` escapes its `new` argument but not `old` ([`__init__.py#L257-L258`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L257-L258)), and `ljust`, `rjust`, `center` escape the fill character ([`__init__.py#L260-L264`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L260-L264), [`#L272-L273`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L272-L273)). Methods that *search* deliberately do not: `strip`/`lstrip`/`rstrip` ([`__init__.py#L266-L276`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L266-L276)), `removeprefix`/`removesuffix` ([`#L297-L301`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L297-L301)) and `partition`/`rpartition` ([`#L303-L311`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L303-L311)) pass their argument through untouched. That was a breaking change in 3.0.0, made so these line up with `in`, `find` and `index`, which never escaped ([`CHANGES.rst#L55-L60`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/CHANGES.rst#L55-L60)). The rule is defensible — you are matching against existing escaped text, not adding to it — but it is a rule a reviewer has to carry in their head, and code written against 2.x may be relying on the old behaviour. > **For the owner:** The sharper edge is that slicing and splitting return `Markup` pieces without checking what they cut: `__getitem__` ([`__init__.py#L242-L243`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L242-L243)), `split`, `rsplit` and `splitlines` ([`#L173-L186`](https://github.com/pallets/markupsafe/blob/b2e4d9c7687be25695fffbe93a37622302b24fb1/src/markupsafe/__init__.py#L173-L186)) each wrap their results in `self.__class__`. In this footer, `<script>` is 12 characters standing for 8; truncating it for a preview can leave a dangling `<scr`, which is well-typed `Markup` and malformed HTML. It is not an injection — the entity is still inert — but it is output you would not want shipped. If anywhere in the codebase truncates or slices rendered markup, flag it: truncate the plain text *before* escaping, not after. Everything in this chapter has only added safety: escaped operands, preserved tags, a type that says so. The next step in the scenario asks for the opposite — the plain-text view of the page — and that is the one operation here that gives the entities back. > **Leaves as:** `Markup('
</p> & <script>oops</script>
')` ```python proof """Replay the scenario through the footer concatenation (trace lines 1-91).""" from markupsafe import Markup, escape class User: def __init__(self, id, name): self.id = id self.name = name def __html_format__(self, format_spec): if format_spec == "link": return Markup('{}').format(self.id, self.__html__()) elif format_spec: raise ValueError("Invalid format spec") return self.__html__() def __html__(self): return Markup('{0}').format(self.name) # --- Chapters 1-4, so the footer starts from the same world --------------- untrusted_comment = "" safe_comment = escape(untrusted_comment) assert safe_comment == "<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>" assert escape(safe_comment) == safe_comment # idempotent user = User(3, 'Alice "The Great"') template = Markup("

User: {user:link} said: {comment}

") page = template.format(user=user, comment=safe_comment) assert page == ( '

User: ' "Alice "The <b>Great</b>"" " said: <script>alert(document.cookie);</script>

" ) assert type(page) is Markup # --- Chapter 5: trace lines 62-91 ---------------------------------------- # line 62: the literal is wrapped, not escaped. opening = Markup("
") assert opening == "
" # lines 64-70: __add__ escapes the plain-str operand via Markup.escape. payload = "

& " escaped_payload = Markup.escape(payload) assert escaped_payload == "</p> & <script>oops</script>" assert type(escaped_payload) is Markup # The bare "&" became "&" exactly once -- no double escaping. assert "&" not in escaped_payload # lines 71-73: the intermediate value. partial = opening + payload assert partial == "
</p> & <script>oops</script>" assert type(partial) is Markup # lines 77-86: escaping an already-safe operand changes nothing. closing = Markup("
") assert Markup.escape(closing) == "
" assert closing.__html__() is closing # lines 87-91: the finished footer and its repr. footer = partial + closing assert footer == "
</p> & <script>oops</script>
" assert type(footer) is Markup assert repr(footer) == ( "Markup('
</p> & <script>oops</script>
')" ) # --- Roads not taken, asserted so the story's claims can fail ------------- # A non-str, non-__html__ operand is refused rather than stringified. assert Markup("a").__add__(3) is NotImplemented try: Markup("a") + 3 except TypeError: pass else: raise AssertionError("expected TypeError for Markup + int") # __radd__: a plain str on the left is escaped too. assert "

" + Markup("
") == "</p>
" # Search-style methods do NOT escape their argument; insertion-style do. assert Markup("x").replace("x", "") == "<b>" assert Markup("-").join(["", Markup("")]) == "<a>-" assert Markup("xa x").removeprefix("x") == "a x" # Slicing a Markup can cut an entity in half and still return Markup. sliced = escaped_payload[:7] assert sliced == "</p&" assert type(sliced) is Markup print("chapter 5 verified") ```
